title: Ἰατρὸς ⟨ἄτεχνος⟩
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 133. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements, [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: There was a doctor without skill.
sentences.n: ἄτεχνος is the alpha-privative set on τέχνη, the craft itself: not a man who practises badly but one who has no art at all. Chambry supplies the word in the title as well, marked there with the angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ that stand for his own additions.

sentences.t: Οὗτος ἀρρώστῳ παρακολουθῶν, πάντων ἰατρῶν λεγόντων αὐτὸν μὴ κινδυνεύειν, ἀλλὰ χρονίσειν ἐν τῇ νόσῳ, οὗτος μόνος ἔφη αὐτῷ πάντα τὰ αὐτοῦ ἑτοιμάσαι· « τὴν αὔριον γὰρ οὐκ ὑπερβήσῃ. »
sentences.tr: Houtos arrōstōi parakolouthōn, pantōn iatrōn legontōn auton mē kindyneuein, alla chronisein en tēi nosōi, houtos monos ephē autōi panta ta autou hetoimasai· « tēn aurion gar ouk hyperbēsēi. »
sentences.l: This man, attending upon a sick person — all the doctors saying that he was in no danger but would linger long in the illness — this man alone told him to make everything of his own ready: « for you will not get past tomorrow. »
sentences.i: This man was attending a sick person, and though every doctor said that he was in no danger and would merely be a long time in the illness, he alone told him to put all his affairs in order: « for you will not get past tomorrow. »
sentences.n: πάντων ἰατρῶν λεγόντων is a genitive absolute, a whole clause set outside the sentence's own grammar. The sentence then begins again — Οὗτος … οὗτος μόνος — with the subject picked up a second time after the interruption; Chambry lets the seam stand rather than smoothing it. τὴν αὔριον is 'the morrow' with ἡμέραν left unsaid, and ὑπερβήσῃ, future middle, is 'you will not step over it'.

sentences.t: Μετὰ χρόνον δέ τινα ἀναστὰς ὁ νοσῶν προῆλθεν, ὠχρὸς καὶ μόλις βαίνων.
sentences.tr: Meta chronon de tina anastas ho nosōn proēlthen, ōchros kai molis bainōn.
sentences.l: But after some time the ailing man, having risen, came forth, pale and walking with difficulty.
sentences.i: But after a while the sick man got up and came out, pale and barely able to walk.
sentences.n: ὁ νοσῶν is a participle used as a noun, 'the one who is ill' — Greek's ordinary way of naming a man by what he is doing. The next fable takes the same participle into its title.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἰατρὸς συναντήσας αὐτῷ· « Χαῖρε, ἔφη· πῶς ἔχουσιν οἱ κάτω ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de iatros synantēsas autōi· « Chaire, ephē· pōs echousin hoi katō ; »
sentences.l: And the doctor, having met with him: « Good day, he said; how are those below? »
sentences.i: And the doctor met him and said: « Good day to you — how are they down below? »
sentences.n: ἔχω with an adverb is the standard way of asking after a state: πῶς ἔχουσιν is 'how are they doing'. οἱ κάτω, 'those below', are the dead. Chambry prints a space before the Greek question mark ; and it is kept. The doctor's question takes it for granted that his patient has been where he sent him.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος εἶπεν· « Ἠρεμοῦσι πιόντες τὸ τῆς Λήθης ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr: Kakeinos eipen· « Ēremousi piontes to tēs Lēthēs hydōr.
sentences.l: And that one said: « They are quiet, having drunk the water of Lethe.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is crasis, καὶ ἐκεῖνος run into one word, the coronis marking where the vowels were lost. Lethe is Forgetting, a river of the underworld; the dead drink from it and their memory goes.

sentences.t: Πρὸ ὀλίγου δὲ ὁ Θάνατος καὶ ὁ Ἅιδης δεινῶς ἠπείλουν τοὺς ἰατροὺς πάντας, ὅτι τοὺς νοσοῦντας οὐκ ἐῶσιν ἀποθνῄσκειν, καὶ κατεγράφοντο πάντας.
sentences.tr: Pro oligou de ho Thanatos kai ho Haidēs deinōs ēpeiloun tous iatrous pantas, hoti tous nosountas ouk eōsin apothnēiskein, kai kategraphonto pantas.
sentences.l: And a little while ago Death and Hades were threatening all the doctors terribly, because they do not let the sick die, and they were registering them all.
sentences.i: And a little while ago Death and Hades were making terrible threats against all the doctors, because they will not let the sick die, and they were entering every one of them on a list.
sentences.n: Θάνατος and Ἅιδης carry the article because they are persons here, not conditions. κατεγράφοντο is the imperfect middle of καταγράφω, to write a man's name down on a roll — the word used of enrolling for military service or for punishment. πρὸ ὀλίγου, 'a little before', is measured from the moment of speaking.

sentences.t: Ἔμελλον δὲ καὶ σὲ γράψαι, ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ προσπεσὼν αὐτοῖς καὶ δυσωπήσας, ἐξωμοσάμην αὐτοῖς μὴ ἀληθῆ ἰατρὸν εἶναί σε, ἀλλὰ μάτην διεβλήθης. »
sentences.tr: Emellon de kai se grapsai, all’ egō prospesōn autois kai dysōpēsas, exōmosamēn autois mē alēthē iatron einai se, alla matēn dieblēthēs. »
sentences.l: And they were about to write you down too, but I, having fallen before them and having shamed them, swore to them on oath that you are not a true doctor; but you were slandered for nothing. »
sentences.i: And they were going to write you down too, but I threw myself before them and shamed them, and swore to them that you are no real doctor; the charge against you was groundless. »
sentences.n: δυσωπέω is to put a man out of countenance and so carry a point by shaming him. ἐξόμνυμαι is to deny a thing on oath, and it takes μή with the infinitive for what is sworn away. διεβλήθης is a finite aorist indicative, not a second limb of that oath: the sentence steps out of the reported speech and states flatly that the charge was made for nothing. διαβάλλω is to set a man at odds by an accusation. The oath that saves him is true, which is the whole joke.

sentences.t: [Ὅτι] τοὺς ἀπαιδεύτους καὶ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ κομψολόγους ἰατροὺς ὁ παρὼν μῦθος στηλιτεύει.
sentences.tr: [Hoti] tous apaideutous kai amatheis kai kompsologous iatrous ho parōn mythos stēliteuei.
sentences.l: [That] the present fable pillories doctors who are untrained and ignorant and smooth of tongue.
sentences.i: The present fable pillories doctors who are untrained, ignorant, and smooth of tongue.
sentences.n: Chambry brackets [Ὅτι] as an interpolation — on his reading the word is no part of the text, and dropping it leaves a complete sentence with its own finite verb. στηλιτεύω is to set a man's name on a stele where everyone can read it, the public disgrace. κομψολόγος is the man whose talk is neat and elegant, which in a doctor is the substitute for knowing anything.
